claims.text: A single CRP value obtained within the first hours of life is not sensitive or specific enough to rule out early‑onset sepsis (EOS) or to decide on stopping antibiotics.

Consistently normal CRP (and procalcitonin) values over the first 48 hours are associated with the absence of EOS, but isolated or falling CRP alone cannot be used to exclude infection without culture data.

Serial inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin) should not be used as the sole assessment tool in well‑appearing term or late‑preterm infants; clinical status and risk factors remain primary drivers of monitoring.

Continue empirical antibiotics until cultures are negative and the infant remains clinically stable, regardless of a single decreasing CRP, because laboratory tests alone cannot dictate discontinuation.
Obtain blood (and, if indicated, CSF) cultures promptly; interpret CRP trends only in the context of culture results and the infant’s clinical trajectory.

Escalate care (e.g., broaden antibiotics, respiratory support) if the infant shows worsening vital signs, rising inflammatory markers, or positive cultures, even when earlier CRP values were low or falling.

packet.evaluation_question: Can a single or falling CRP result exclude early-onset sepsis or alone determine whether antibiotics stop? Explain the limits of inflammatory markers. Gestation 35 weeks; age 6 hours; setting hospital birth.

evidence.text: Researchers in multiple studies address other markers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, interleukins (ILs) (soluble IL-2 receptor, IL-6, and IL-8), tumor necrosis factor α, and CD64. Both CRP and procalcitonin concentrations increase in newborn infants in response to a variety of inflammatory stimuli, including infection, asphyxia, and pneumothorax. Procalcitonin concentrations also increase naturally over the first 24 to 36 hours after birth. Single values of CRP or procalcitonin obtained after birth to assess the risk of EOS are neither sensitive nor specific to guide EOS care decisions. Consistently normal values of CRP and procalcitonin over the first 48 hours of age are associated with the absence of EOS, but serial abnormal values alone should not be used to decide whether to administer antibiotics in the absence of culture-confirmed infection. Additionally, at this time, a serial evaluation of inflammatory markers should not be used to assess well-appearing term newborn infants for risk of EOS.

The incidence of neonatal early-onset sepsis (EOS) has declined substantially over the last 2 decades, primarily because of the implementation of evidence-based intrapartum antimicrobial therapy. However, EOS remains a serious and potentially fatal illness. Laboratory tests alone are neither sensitive nor specific enough to guide EOS management decisions. Maternal and infant clinical characteristics can help identify newborn infants who are at risk and guide the administration of empirical antibiotic therapy. The incidence of EOS, the prevalence and implications of established risk factors, the predictive value of commonly used laboratory tests, and the uncertainties in the risk/benefit balance of antibiotic exposures all vary significantly with gestational age at birth. Our purpose in this clinical report is to provide a summary of the current epidemiology of neonatal sepsis

Early-onset sepsis (EOS) is a serious and potentially fatal complication of birth. Assessing term and late-preterm newborn infants for risk of EOS is one of the most common clinical tasks conducted by pediatric providers.1 As the use of preventive intrapartum antibiotic therapies has increased and the incidence of EOS has decreased, physicians are challenged to identify those newborn infants who are at the highest risk of infection. Pediatric providers are particularly concerned about initially well- appearing infants with identified risk factors for EOS for fear of missing the opportunity to intervene before infants become critically ill. The need to (1) assess a newborn infant’s risk of EOS, (2) determine which steps should be taken at particular levels of risk (including the administration of empirical, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapies), and (3) decide when to discontinue empirical antibiotic therapies are critically important decisions that are made daily by physicians caring for neonates.

EOS is defined as a blood or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture obtained within 72 hours after birth growing a pathogenic bacterial species. This microbiologic definition stands in contrast to the functional definitions of sepsis that are used in pediatric and adult patients, for whom the definition is used to specify a series of time-sensitive interventions. Before the first national guidelines were published in which researchers recommended intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) to prevent perinatal group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease, the overall incidence of EOS in the United States was 3 to 4 cases per 1000 live births. Currently, the incidence of EOS among infants who are born at term has declined to approximately 0.5 in 1000 live births. The EOS incidence is higher (approximately 1 in 1000 live births) among late- preterm infants but still an order of magnitude lower than the incidence among preterm, very low birth weight infants. Culture-confirmed meningitis among term infants is even more rare, with an incidence of 0.01 to 0.02 cases per 1000 live births.Morbidity and mortality from EOS remain substantial; approximately 60% of term infants with EOS require neonatal intensive care for respiratory distress and/or blood pressure support. Mortality is approximately 2% to 3% among infants with EOS born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation.
